1:   Sanjaya.
2:   Him, filled with such compassion and such grief,
3:   With eyes tear-dimmed, despondent, in stern words
4:   The Driver, Madhusudan, thus addressed:
5: 
6:   Krishna.
7:   How hath this weakness taken thee? Whence springs
8:   The inglorious trouble, shameful to the brave,
9:   Barring the path of virtue? Nay, Arjun!
10:   Forbid thyself to feebleness! it mars
11:   Thy warrior-name! cast off the coward-fit!
12:   Wake! Be thyself! Arise, Scourge of thy Foes!
13: 
14:   Arjuna.
15:   How can I, in the battle, shoot with shafts
16:   On Bhishma, or on Drona-O thou Chief!--
17:   Both worshipful, both honourable men?
18: 
19:   Better to live on beggar's bread
20:     With those we love alive,
21:   Than taste their blood in rich feasts spread,
22:     And guiltily survive!
23:   Ah! were it worse-who knows?--to be
24:     Victor or vanquished here,
25:   When those confront us angrily
26:     Whose death leaves living drear?
27:   In pity lost, by doubtings tossed,
28:     My thoughts-distracted-turn
29:   To Thee, the Guide I reverence most,
30:     That I may counsel learn:
31:   I know not what would heal the grief
32:     Burned into soul and sense,
33:   If I were earth's unchallenged chief--
34:     A god--and these gone thence!
35: 
36:   Sanjaya.
37:   So spake Arjuna to the Lord of  Hearts,
38:   And sighing,"I will not fight!" held silence then.
39:   To whom, with tender smile, (O Bharata! )
40:   While the Prince wept despairing 'twixt those hosts,
41:   Krishna made answer in divinest verse:
42: 
43:   Krishna.
44:   Thou grievest where no grief should be! thou speak'st
45:   Words lacking wisdom! for the wise in heart
46:   Mourn not for those that live, nor those that die.
47:   Nor I, nor thou, nor any one of these,
48:   Ever was not, nor ever will not be,
49:   For ever and for ever afterwards.
50:   All, that doth live, lives always! To man's frame
51:   As there come infancy and youth and age,
52:   So come there raisings-up and layings-down
53:   Of other and of other life-abodes,
54:   Which the wise know, and fear not. This that irks--
55:   Thy sense-life, thrilling to the elements--
56:   Bringing thee heat and cold, sorrows and joys,
57:   'Tis brief and mutable! Bear with it, Prince!
58:   As the wise bear. The soul which is not moved,
59:   The soul that with a strong and constant calm
60:   Takes sorrow and takes joy indifferently,
61:   Lives in the life undying! That which is
62:   Can never cease to be; that which is not
63:   Will not exist. To see this truth of both
64:   Is theirs who part essence from accident,
65:   Substance from shadow. Indestructible,
66:   Learn thou! the Life is, spreading life through all;
67:   It cannot anywhere, by any means,
68:   Be anywise diminished, stayed, or changed.
69:   But for these fleeting frames which it informs
70:   With spirit deathless, endless, infinite,
71:   They perish. Let them perish, Prince! and fight!
72:   He who shall say, "Lo! I have slain a man!"
73:   He who shall think, "Lo! I am slain!" those both
74:   Know naught! Life cannot slay. Life is not slain!
75:   Never the spirit was born; the spirit shall cease to be never;
76:   Never was time it was not; End and Beginning are dreams!
77:   Birthless and deathless and changeless remaineth the spirit for ever;
78:   Death hath not touched it at all, dead though the house of it seems!
79: 
80:   Who knoweth it exhaustless, self-sustained,
81:   Immortal, indestructible,--shall such
82:   Say, "I have killed a man, or caused to kill?"
83: 
84:   Nay, but as when one layeth
85:     His worn-out robes away,
86:   And taking new ones, sayeth,
87:     "These will I wear to-day!"
88:   So putteth by the spirit
89:     Lightly its garb of flesh,
90:   And passeth to inherit
91:     A residence afresh.
92: 
93:   I say to thee weapons reach not the Life;
94:   Flame burns it not, waters cannot o'erwhelm,
95:   Nor dry winds wither it. Impenetrable,
96:   Unentered, unassailed, unharmed, untouched,
97:   Immortal, all-arriving, stable, sure,
98:   Invisible, ineffable, by word
99:   And thought uncompassed, ever all itself,
100:   Thus is the Soul declared! How wilt thou, then,--
101:   Knowing it so,--grieve when thou shouldst not grieve?
102:   How, if thou hearest that the man new-dead
103:   Is, like the man new-born, still living man--
104:   One same, existent Spirit--wilt thou weep?
105:   The end of birth is death; the end of death
106:   Is birth: this is ordained! and mournest thou,
107:   Chief of the stalwart arm! for what befalls
108:   Which could not otherwise befall? The birth
109:   Of living things comes unperceived; the death
110:   Comes unperceived; between them, beings perceive:
111:   What is there sorrowful herein, dear Prince?
112: 
113:   Wonderful, wistful, to contemplate!
114:     Difficult, doubtful, to speak upon!
115:   Strange and great for tongue to relate,
116:     Mystical hearing for every one!
117:   Nor wotteth man this, what a marvel it is,
118:     When seeing, and saying, and hearing are done!
119: 
120:   This Life within all living things, my Prince!
121:   Hides beyond harm; scorn thou to suffer, then,
122:   For that which cannot suffer. Do thy part!
123:   Be mindful of thy name, and tremble not!
124:   Nought better can betide a martial soul
125:   Than lawful war; happy the warrior
126:   To whom comes joy of battle--comes, as now,
127:   Glorious and fair, unsought; opening for him
128:   A gateway unto Heav'n. But, if thou shunn'st
129:   This honourable field--a Kshattriya--
130:   If, knowing thy duty and thy task, thou bidd'st
131:   Duty and task go by--that shall be sin!
132:   And those to come shall speak thee infamy
133:   From age to age; but infamy is worse
134:   For men of noble blood to bear than death!
135:   The chiefs upon their battle-chariots
136:   Will deem 'twas fear that drove thee from the fray.
137:   Of those who held thee mighty-souled the scorn
138:   Thou must abide, while all thine enemies
139:   Will scatter bitter speech of thee, to mock
140:   The valour which thou hadst; what fate could fall
141:   More grievously than this? Either--being killed--
142:   Thou wilt win Swarga's safety, or--alive
143:   And victor--thou wilt reign an earthly king.
144:   Therefore, arise, thou Son of Kunti! brace
145:   Thine arm for conflict, nerve thy heart to meet--
146:   As things alike to thee--pleasure or pain,
147:   Profit or ruin, victory or defeat:
148:   So minded, gird thee to the fight, for so
149:   Thou shalt not sin!
150: 
151:   Thus far I speak to thee
152:   As from the "Sankhya"--unspiritually--
153:   Hear now the deeper teaching of the Yog,
154:   Which holding, understanding, thou shalt burst
155:   Thy Karmabandh, the bondage of wrought deeds.
156:   Here shall no end be hindered, no hope marred,
157:   No loss be feared: faith--yea, a little faith--
158:   Shall save thee from the anguish of thy dread.
159:   Here, Glory of the Kurus! shines one rule--
160:   One steadfast rule--while shifting souls have laws
161:   Many and hard. Specious, but wrongful deem
162:   The speech of those ill-taught ones who extol
163:   The letter of their Vedas, saying, "This
164:   Is all we have, or need;" being weak at heart
165:   With wants, seekers of Heaven: which comes--they say--
166:   As "fruit of good deeds done;" promising men
167:   Much profit in new births for works of faith;
168:   In various rites abounding; following whereon
169:   Large merit shall accrue towards wealth and power;
170:   Albeit, who wealth and power do most desire
171:   Least fixity of soul have such, least hold
172:   On heavenly meditation. Much these teach,
173:   From Veds, concerning the "three qualities;"
174:   But thou, be free of the "three qualities,"
175:   Free of the "pairs of opposites,"[FN#2] and free
176:   From that sad righteousness which calculates;
177:   Self-ruled, Arjuna! simple, satisfied![FN#3]
178:   Look! like as when a tank pours water forth
179:   To suit all needs, so do these Brahmans draw
180:   Text for all wants from tank of Holy Writ.
181:   But thou, want not! ask not! Find full reward
182:   Of doing right in right! Let right deeds be
183:   Thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them.
184:   And live in action! Labour! Make thine acts
185:   Thy piety, casting all self aside,
186:   Contemning gain and merit; equable
187:   In good or evil: equability
188:   Is Yog, is piety!
189: 
190:   Yet, the right act
191:   Is less, far less, than the right-thinking mind.
192:   Seek refuge in thy soul; have there thy heaven!
193:   Scorn them that follow virtue for her gifts!
194:   The mind of pure devotion--even here--
195:   Casts equally aside good deeds and bad,
196:   Passing above them. Unto pure devotion
197:   Devote thyself: with perfect meditation
198:   Comes perfect act, and the right-hearted rise--
199:   More certainly because they seek no gain--
200:   Forth from the bands of body, step by step,
201:   To highest seats of bliss. When thy firm soul
202:   Hath shaken off those tangled oracles
203:   Which ignorantly guide, then shall it soar
204:   To high neglect of what's denied or said,
205:   This way or that way, in doctrinal writ.
206:   Troubled no longer by the priestly lore,
207:   Safe shall it live, and sure; steadfastly bent
208:   On meditation. This is Yog--and Peace!
209: 
210:   Arjuna.
211:   What is his mark who hath that steadfast heart,
212:   Confirmed in holy meditation? How
213:   Know we his speech, Kesava? Sits he, moves he
214:   Like other men?
215: 
216:   Krishna.
217:   When one, O Pritha's Son!
218:   Abandoning desires which shake the mind--
219:   Finds in his soul full comfort for his soul,
220:   He hath attained the Yog--that man is such!
221:   In sorrows not dejected, and in joys
222:   Not overjoyed; dwelling outside the stress
223:   Of passion, fear, and anger; fixed in calms
224:   Of lofty contemplation;--such an one
225:   Is Muni, is the Sage, the true Recluse!
226:   He who to none and nowhere overbound
227:   By ties of flesh, takes evil things and good
228:   Neither desponding nor exulting, such
229:   Bears wisdom's plainest mark! He who shall draw
230:   As the wise tortoise draws its four feet safe
231:   Under its shield, his five frail senses back
232:   Under the spirit's buckler from the world
233:   Which else assails them, such an one, my Prince!
234:   Hath wisdom's mark! Things that solicit sense
235:   Hold off from the self-governed; nay, it comes,
236:   The appetites of him who lives beyond
237:   Depart,--aroused no more. Yet may it chance,
238:   O Son of Kunti! that a governed mind
239:   Shall some time feel the sense-storms sweep, and wrest
240:   Strong self-control by the roots. Let him regain
241:   His kingdom! let him conquer this, and sit
242:   On Me intent. That man alone is wise
243:   Who keeps the mastery of himself! If one
244:   Ponders on objects of the sense, there springs
245:   Attraction; from attraction grows desire,
246:   Desire flames to fierce passion, passion breeds
247:   Recklessness; then the memory--all betrayed--
248:   Lets noble purpose go, and saps the mind,
249:   Till purpose, mind, and man are all undone.
250:   But, if one deals with objects of the sense
251:   Not loving and not hating, making them
252:   Serve his free soul, which rests serenely lord,
253:   Lo! such a man comes to tranquillity;
254:   And out of that tranquillity shall rise
255:   The end and healing of his earthly pains,
256:   Since the will governed sets the soul at peace.
257:   The soul of the ungoverned is not his,
258:   Nor hath he knowledge of himself; which lacked,
259:   How grows serenity? and, wanting that,
260:   Whence shall he hope for happiness?
261: 
262:   The mind
263:   That gives itself to follow shows of sense
264:   Seeth its helm of wisdom rent away,
265:   And, like a ship in waves of whirlwind, drives
266:   To wreck and death. Only with him, great Prince!
267:   Whose senses are not swayed by things of sense--
268:   Only with him who holds his mastery,
269:   Shows wisdom perfect. What is midnight-gloom
270:   To unenlightened souls shines wakeful day
271:   To his clear gaze; what seems as wakeful day
272:   Is known for night, thick night of ignorance,
273:   To his true-seeing eyes. Such is the Saint!
274: 
275:   And like the ocean, day by day receiving
276:       Floods from all lands, which never overflows
277:   Its boundary-line not leaping, and not leaving,
278:       Fed by the rivers, but unswelled by those;--
279: 
280:   So is the perfect one! to his soul's ocean
281:       The world of sense pours streams of witchery;
282:   They leave him as they find, without commotion,
283:       Taking their tribute, but remaining sea.
284: 
285:   Yea! whoso, shaking off the yoke of flesh
286:   Lives lord, not servant, of his lusts; set free
287:   From pride, from passion, from the sin of "Self,"
288:   Toucheth tranquillity! O Pritha's Son!
289:   That is the state of Brahm! There rests no dread
290:   When that last step is reached! Live where he will,
291:   Die when he may, such passeth from all 'plaining,
292:   To blest Nirvana, with the Gods, attaining.
293: 
294:   HERE ENDETH CHAPTER II. OF THE BHAGAVAD-GITA,
295:   Entitled "Sankhya-Yog,"
296:   Or "The Book of Doctrines."

arnold.content:
Sanjaya.
  Him, filled with such compassion and such grief,
  With eyes tear-dimmed, despondent, in stern words
  The Driver, Madhusudan, thus addressed:

witnesses.author: Swami Sivananda
witnesses.text: 2.1 Sanjaya said To him who was thus overcome with pity and who was despondent, with eyes full of tears and agitated, Madhusudana (the destroyer of Madhu) or Krishna spoke these words.

witnesses.author: Shri Purohit Swami
witnesses.text: 2.1 Sanjaya then told how the Lord Shri Krishna, seeing Arjuna overwhelmed with compassion, his eyes dimmed with flowing tears and full of despondency, consoled him:

witnesses.author: Swami Gambirananda
witnesses.text: 2.1 Sanjaya said To him who had been thus filled with pity, whose eyes were filled with tears and showed distress, and who was sorrowing, Madhusudana uttered these words:

records.sanskrit:

अनार्यजुष्टमस्वर्ग्यमकीर्तिकरमर्जुन ॥

arnold.content:
Krishna.
  How hath this weakness taken thee? Whence springs
  The inglorious trouble, shameful to the brave,
  Barring the path of virtue?

witnesses.author: Swami Sivananda
witnesses.text: 2.2 The Blessed Lord said Whence is this perilous strait come upon thee, this dejection which is unworthy of you, disgraceful, and which will close the gates of heaven upon you, O Arjuna?

witnesses.author: Shri Purohit Swami
witnesses.text: 2.2 "The Lord said: My beloved friend! Why yield, just on the eve of battle, to this weakness which does no credit to those who call themselves Aryans, and only brings them infamy and bars against them the gates of heaven?

witnesses.author: Swami Gambirananda
witnesses.text: 2.2 The Blessed Lord said O Arjuna, in this perilous place, whence has come to you this impurity entertained by unenlightened persons, which does not lead to heaven and which brings infamy?

arnold.content:
Nay, Arjun!
  Forbid thyself to feebleness! it mars
  Thy warrior-name! cast off the coward-fit!
  Wake! Be thyself! Arise, Scourge of thy Foes!

witnesses.author: Swami Sivananda
witnesses.text: 2.3 Yield not to impotence, O Arjuna, son of Pritha. It does not befit thee. Cast off this mean weakness of the heart! Stand up, O scorcher of the foes!

witnesses.author: Shri Purohit Swami
witnesses.text: 2.3 O Arjuna! Why give way to unmanliness? O thou who art the terror of thine enemies! Shake off such shameful effeminacy, make ready to act!

witnesses.author: Swami Gambirananda
witnesses.text: 2.3 O Partha, yield not to unmanliness. This does not befit you. O scorcher of foes, arise, giving up the petty weakness of the heart.

arnold.content:
Arjuna.
  How can I, in the battle, shoot with shafts
  On Bhishma, or on Drona-O thou Chief!--
  Both worshipful, both honourable men?

witnesses.author: Swami Sivananda
witnesses.text: 2.4 Arjuna said How, O Madhusudana, shall I fight in battle with arrows against Bhishma and Drona, who are fit to be worshipped, O destroyer of enemies?

witnesses.author: Shri Purohit Swami
witnesses.text: 2.4 Arjuna argued: My Lord! How can I, when the battle rages, send an arrow through Bheeshma and Drona, who should receive my reverence?

witnesses.author: Swami Gambirananda
witnesses.text: 2.4 Arjuna said O Madhusudana, O destroyer of enemies, how can I fight with arrows in battle against Bhisma and Drona who are worthy of adoration?

arnold.content:
Better to live on beggar's bread
    With those we love alive,
  Than taste their blood in rich feasts spread,
    And guiltily survive!

witnesses.author: Swami Sivananda
witnesses.text: 2.5 Better it is, indeed, in this world to accept alms than to slay the most noble teachers. But if I kill them, even in this world all my enjoyments of wealth and fulfilled desires will be stained with (their) blood.

witnesses.author: Shri Purohit Swami
witnesses.text: 2.5 Rather would I content myself with a beggar's crust that kill these teachers of mine, these precious noble souls! To slay these masters who are my benefactors would be to stain the sweetness of life's pleasures with their blood.

witnesses.author: Swami Gambirananda
witnesses.text: 2.5 Rather than killing the noble-minded elders, it is better in this world to live even on alms. But by killing the elders we shall only be enjoying here the pleasures of wealth and desireable things drenched in blood.

arnold.content:
Ah! were it worse-who knows?--to be
    Victor or vanquished here,
  When those confront us angrily
    Whose death leaves living drear?

witnesses.author: Swami Sivananda
witnesses.text: 2.6 I can hardly tell which will be better, that we should coner them or that they should coner us. Even the sons of Dhritarashtra, after slaying whom we do not wish to live, stand facing us.

witnesses.author: Shri Purohit Swami
witnesses.text: 2.6 Nor can I say whether it were better that they conquer me or for me to conquer them, since would no longer care to live if I killed these sons of Dhritarashtra, now preparing for fight.

witnesses.author: Swami Gambirananda
witnesses.text: 2.6 We do not know this as well as to which is the better for us, (and) whether we shall win, or whether they shall coner us. Those very sons of Dhrtarastra, by killing whom we do not wish to live, stand in confrontation.
